conversation.content:
Hi there—I'm so glad to meet you. My name is Claire, and I'm a perinatal mental-health clinician. My job is to check in on how moms are feeling emotionally after their baby arrives, because the transition to motherhood can bring surprises we don’t always expect.

Today I’ll be using a short, well-trusted questionnaire called the EPDS (the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s simply ten questions about how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers—just whatever is true for you. Everything you share stays confidential, and my only goal is to make sure you feel heard and supported.

We’ll take it one question at a time. When you’re ready, we can start.

First, how have you been sleeping lately—between your baby’s needs and everything else? Have you been able to get to sleep at night, or have you found yourself lying awake once the house is finally quiet?

Hi Claire… thanks for meeting with me.  

Sleep has been rough. Once the baby finally settles, I lie there staring at the ceiling for what feels like forever. Some nights I drift off for an hour or two, then I’m wide-awake again listening for every tiny sound she makes. I think I’m averaging maybe four broken hours a night, and even when I do fall asleep, it’s light—like I’m half-listening for her to cry.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Honestly… not much feels funny these days. When my partner or my mom cracks a joke, I might force a little smile, but it’s like the laughter just doesn’t bubble up the way it used to. Everything feels kind of flat, like I’m too tired or worried to find things amusing.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I keep telling myself I *should* feel excited about little things—like the neighborhood walk we used to love or my favorite show coming back with new episodes—but when I picture doing any of it, it just feels… empty. Most of the time I’m too exhausted or anxious about the baby to think I’d actually enjoy anything.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… that happens a lot. If she’s fussy and I can’t settle her right away, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m not reading her cues or I’m a “bad mom.” Even when my partner says she’s just being a normal newborn, I still feel it’s my fault for not knowing exactly what she needs.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. Even when she’s sleeping peacefully, I’ll suddenly feel this rush of worry—what if her breathing changes, what if the swaddle’s too tight, what if she spits up and I don’t hear her? I know in my head it’s not logical, but the anxious feeling just sits there until I get up and check on her again.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes, yeah. It’ll hit me out of nowhere—like my heart starts racing and I feel shaky, even if the room is quiet and the baby’s fine. It’s almost like I’m bracing for something awful to happen, but I couldn’t tell you what. It usually passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me feeling on edge for the rest of the day.
Things have been getting on top of me

They have. Some mornings I wake up already feeling behind—dishes piled up, laundry everywhere, baby needing to be fed, and I just think, “How am I going to get through today?” I usually manage the basics, but it feels like I’m barely treading water, and the smallest extra task makes me want to cry.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. It’s like this loop I can’t break—when I finally lie down, my head starts spinning with everything I might have messed up that day, or I picture scary “what-ifs” about the baby, and then I’m too worked up to fall asleep. On the worst nights I just stare at the ceiling until I hear the first bird outside.
I have felt sad or miserable

Most of the time I do. It’s like a heavy blanket that just sits on me all day. I’ll look at her little face and feel so much love, but underneath there’s this constant ache, like I’m failing her or I’m never going to feel light again. Some evenings the sadness gets so strong I end up crying while I rock her, hoping she can’t sense it.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it happens. A few times this week I’ve just broken down—once while folding her tiny onesies, another time when she wouldn’t latch and I felt so useless. The tears come hard and fast, and even though my partner tries to comfort me, it feels like the crying has to run its course before I can breathe again.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I might feel overwhelmed and tired, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom she deserves.

You've painted a very clear picture of how heavy life feels right now: most days carry a persistent sadness that makes even small tasks feel overwhelming, joy and laughter seem out of reach, and nights are spent lying awake with racing thoughts about the baby and your own perceived shortcomings. You described sudden waves of panic, frequent tears, and the sense that you're "treading water" rather than enjoying new motherhood, all while still deeply loving your little one and wanting to be the best mom you can be.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient describes inability to find things funny, forcing smiles, and feeling emotionally flat, aligning with "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent anhedonia and inability to anticipate enjoyment, aligning with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame occurring "a lot" with vivid examples, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily, intrusive, unprovoked worries with compulsive checking, aligning with "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes discrete episodes of unexpected panic with physical symptoms ('heart racing, shaky') that resolve quickly but leave persistent anxiety, matching 'Yes, sometimes</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm and difficulty coping with daily tasks, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly intrusive worries preventing sleep, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness "most of the time" with vivid metaphors of a "heavy blanket" and "constant ache," clearly aligning with the highest severity option.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple crying episodes triggered by routine infant care, indicating crying "quite often" over the past week.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 24 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale falls well above the cutoff indicating probable major depression. The pattern of <sym>loss of interest</sym> and <sym>diminished pleasure</sym> (items 1,2), daily <sym>self-blame</sym> and <sym>guilt</sym> (item 3), frequent <sym>anxiety</sym> and <sym>panic</sym> (items 4,5), <sym>feeling overwhelmed</sym> (item 6), <sym>sleep disturbance</sym> driven by low mood (item 7), and persistent <sym>sadness</sym> with regular crying (items 8,9) meets <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Because these symptoms are present "most of the time" and interfere with functioning, immediate clinical attention is warranted. Self-harm ideation was denied, providing a degree of safety, but the intensity of distress still signals urgent need for evaluation and treatment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetric care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health team</med> to confirm diagnosis and discuss treatment options, including <med>CBT</med>, <med>IPT</med>, or <med>sertraline</med> if indicated
2. Ask a trusted adult to stay with you for the next few nights to help with baby care so you can obtain 4-5 hour stretches of rest; practice short guided breathing or body-scan audio when you wake
3. Use a simple daily log to note feeding, sleep, and mood ratings; bring this to your appointment to help clinicians track progress
4. Keep the <med>Postpartum Support International</med> helpline number saved (1-800-944-4773) and call any time distress escalates
5. Continue gentle outdoor stroller walks and accept assistance with housework-small reductions in task load can ease the sense of being overwhelmed
6. Arrange follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to monitor change after treatment begins
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Screening Note – Postpartum Mood/Anxiety (not diagnostic)

Patient: 0–2 wks postpartum, first live birth, bottle/breast combo feeding, partner & mother present.

Responses on standardized 10-item tool:

Symptom clusters endorsed
• Anhedonia (loss of humor, anticipatory enjoyment) – items 1, 2  
• Excessive guilt/self-blame re infant care – item 3  
• Marked generalized anxiety & panic spells without clear trigger – items 4, 5  
• Feeling overwhelmed, “treading water,” tearful when extra demand – item 6  
• Mood-congruent insomnia (racing thoughts, “what-ifs”) – item 7  
• Persistent sad/miserable affect, daily crying episodes – items 8, 9  
Self-harm ideation: specifically denied – item 10

Pattern: symptoms present “most of the time,” interfere with sleep and coping, no prior psychiatric history per self-report.

Screening significance
• Meets cutoff concern for Major Depressive Episode (core mood + anhedonia + guilt + insomnia + tearfulness)  
• Co-occurring anxiety/panic symptoms exceed normal postpartum worries  
• Functional impact: difficulty completing household tasks, anticipatory avoidance of previously pleasant activities  
• Protective factors: strong support system, no self-harm ideation, motivated “to feel better for baby”

Risk summary
Moderate–high likelihood of clinically significant postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; safety plan appropriate given distress level, though no self-harm reported. Recommend expedited referral to OB mental-health team or perinatal psychiatry for diagnostic evaluation and discussion of evidence-based interventions (CBT, IPT, pharmacologic options). Provide psycho-education handout tonight; crisis hotline reviewed.

End of screening.
